ety.text: From the given name of Sir Robert Peel, who established London’s police force.

senses.d: A police officer.
A railway signaller.
A penis.
Cocaine.
A calf that is slaughtered in its first month, usually because it has no mother or because it is undersized or otherwise defective.
ex: The following is the Victorian code of practice as it refers to the welfare of bobby calves.
All bobby calves must be fed as close as possible to, and at least within 6 hours of, the time of transportation.

senses.d: A banana that is extra small in size.
ex: My kids like bobby bananas, but they're in plastic.

it:poliziotto.gl: policeman, police officer, cop, copper, rozzer, bobby

ety.text: From piedi + piatti, literally “flat feet”. Calque of American English flatfoot.

es:madero.gl: a piece of wood, a piece of timber

chain.g: to move up and down or back and forth

ety.text: From Middle English bobben (“to move up and down or back and forth”), of uncertain origin. Compare Scots bob (“to mark, dance with a bobbing motion”), Icelandic boppa (“to wave up and down”), Swedish bobba (“to bob”), Faroese bøbbur (“something that rises or stands up; top”), Dutch dobberen (“to float, bob”).

chain.g: a cluster (of fruit); a twig with its leaves, a spray

ety.text: From Middle English bobbe (“a cluster (of fruit); a twig with its leaves, a spray”), perhaps of Celtic origin (compare Irish baban "tassel, cluster," Gaelic babag).

senses.d: To move gently and vertically, in either a single motion or repeatedly up and down, at or near the surface of a body of water, or similar medium.
ex: The cork bobbed gently in the calm water.
The ball, which we had thought lost, suddenly bobbed up out of the water.

senses.d: To move (something) as though it were bobbing in water.
ex: I bobbed my head underwater and saw the goldfish.

senses.d: To perform oral sex on someone.
To curtsy.
To strike with a quick, light blow; to tap.
ex: Lo, lo, lo, lo, what modicums of wit he vtters, his euaſions haue eares thus long, I haue bobd his braine more then he has beate my bones.

senses.d: Synonym of blob (“catch eels using worms strung on thread”).
A bobbing motion; a quick up and down movement.
A curtsy.
A bobber (buoyant fishing device).
ex: Or yellow bobs turn’d up before the plough / Are chiefest baits, with cork and lead enough.

senses.d: Any of various hesperiid butterflies.
A bob haircut.
Any round object attached loosely to a flexible line, a rod, a body part etc., so that it may swing when hanging from it.
ex: Ecod! I have got them. Here they are. My cousin Con's necklaces, bobs and all.

senses.d: The dangling mass of a pendulum or plumb line.
The docked tail of a horse.
The short runner of a sled.
A bobsleigh.
A small wheel, made of leather, with rounded edges, used in polishing spoons, etc.
A working beam in a steam engine.
A particular style of ringing changes on bells.
A blow; a shake or jog; a rap, as with the fist.
To cut (hair) into a bob haircut.
ex: I got my hair bobbed. How do you like it?

senses.d: To shorten by cutting; to dock; to crop.
To bobsleigh.
A shilling.
A 10-cent coin, ten cents.
An unspecified small amount of money.
ex: I could have saved myself a few bob buying it somewhere else.
So what can I do for you? Local charity, is it? Policeman's ball? Widows and orphans? I'm usually good for a bob or two.

senses.d: A graphical element, resembling a hardware sprite, that can be blitted around the screen in large numbers.
ex: The bob list determines the drawing priority […]
IMHO, youd ^([sic]) be better doing other things with the CPU and letting the blitter draw bobs, esp on a machine with fast ram.

ety.text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *undizāre. Derivable from onda + -eggiare.
Possibly from Vulgar Latin *dēundulāre, with onomatopoetic influence of don (“dong (sound of a bell ringing)”).
From tra- + ballare; cognate with Piedmontese trabalé.

it:sballottare.gl: to jolt, bob, toss or throw (about or around)

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French poix, from Old French pois, peis, from Vulgar Latin *pēsum, from Latin pēnsum. Spelling influenced by Latin pondus with the same meaning; both ultimately from the root of pendō (“to weigh”). Doublet of pensum, which was borrowed.
Inherited from Middle French plom, from Old French plom, from Latin plumbum.
